ox: Correct. Discrimination is behavior, here refusing to rent based on ethnicity.
Wrong. Prejudice is the attitude or feeling behind the act, not the act. Trap: confusing the cause with the action.
Wrong. A stereotype is a belief about a group. The landlord is acting, not just believing.
Wrong. Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by your own culture's standards. It is not the action of refusing to rent.

p: These three form a chain. Stereotype is the thought (a belief about a group). Prejudice is the feeling (a negative attitude). Discrimination is the action (unfair treatment).
Refusing to rent is an action, so it is discrimination.

q123.eli: Thinking, feeling, doing. Refusing to rent is the doing.
mem: Stereotype = cognitive (thought).
Prejudice = affective (feeling).
Discrimination = behavioral (action).
q123.mn: Think-Feel-Do (a memory phrase, not an acronym): Stereotype is Think, Prejudice is Feel, Discrimination is Do.
q123.trap: Look for an action word like refuses. Only unfair treatment of people because of their group is discrimination, so check that the action targets a group.
q123.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology and psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Goffman's dramaturgical approach treats life as theater, with a front stage (warm with customers) and a back stage (venting in the kitchen).
Wrong. Cognitive dissonance is discomfort from conflict between beliefs and actions. Nothing here shows that discomfort.
Wrong. Role strain is tension within a single role. The server is switching between settings, not stressed by one role.
Wrong. Symbolic interactionism is the broad theory that meaning comes from social interaction. Dramaturgy is the specific model that fits.

p: Erving Goffman compared social life to a stage play. Impression management means controlling how others see us.
On the front stage we perform a role for an audience. On the back stage we relax and drop the act.

q124.eli: An actor smiles for the crowd, then drops the act backstage.
mem: Front stage = performing for an audience.
Back stage = private, no performance.
Impression management is the core idea.
q124.trap: Choose the specific theory (dramaturgy) over the broad one (symbolic interactionism).
q124.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Age is assigned to you, not earned. Ascribed statuses are given at birth or involuntarily.
Wrong. Becoming a physician takes training and effort, so it is achieved.
Wrong. Graduating is earned, so it is achieved.
Wrong. Being chosen captain depends on merit or choice, so it is achieved.

p: A status is a position in society. Ascribed statuses are assigned without choice or effort, like age, race, or being born into a family.
Achieved statuses are earned or chosen, like jobs and degrees.

q125.eli: You do not choose your birthday, but you earn a trophy.
mem: Ascribed = assigned (age, race, sex, family).
Achieved = earned (degree, job, captain).
Ask: did effort or choice get them here?
q125.trap: Occupations and titles are almost always achieved.
q125.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. She earned it through residency and certification, so it is an achieved status.
Wrong. Ascribed statuses are assigned at birth or involuntarily, like age or race. Surgeon is earned.
Wrong. Master status is a status that dominates how others see a person. Nothing suggests surgeon overrides all her other statuses.
Wrong. Primary describes a type of group (close, personal), not a type of status.

p: A status is a position in society. An achieved status is gained through effort, choices, or merit, such as earning a degree.
Ascribed statuses are assigned without effort. A master status is any status that overshadows all the others.

x8C_001.eli: Earning a black belt takes training. Being born in March does not.
mem: Achieved = earned.
Ascribed = assigned at birth or involuntarily.
Master = dominates how others see you.
x8C_001.trap: Do not choose master just because the job is prestigious. The stem needs a status type about how it was gained.
x8C_001.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. A role set is the group of roles that go with one status, like a teacher's roles with students and parents. It does not mean a dominant label.
Wrong. A criminal record comes from his own actions, so it is not ascribed. Trap: assuming an imposed label means ascribed.
Wrong. A reference group is a group used as a standard to compare yourself against. It is not a status.
Correct. His ex-offender status overshadows his degree and work history. A status that dominates all others is a master status.

p: A master status is the one status that overrides all others and shapes how people treat you. It can be positive or negative.
How it was gained does not matter. What makes it master is that it dominates. This one is achieved, since it came from his own actions.

x8C_002.eli: If everyone only calls you the kid who broke the window, that label hides everything else about you.
mem: Master status = dominates all other statuses.
It can be ascribed or achieved.
Role set = roles tied to one status.
x8C_002.trap: A label that feels imposed is not automatically ascribed. Judge it by how it was gained.
x8C_002.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. A status set is ALL the statuses one person holds (professor, mother, citizen). The trap is mixing up 'many statuses' with 'many roles inside one status'.
Correct. A role set is the group of roles that go with ONE status. The status 'professor' brings teaching, advising and committee roles.
Wrong. Role strain is stress from clashing demands inside a role. The stem lists behaviors but shows no stress, so do not add tension that is not there.
Wrong. A master status is the one status that overshadows all others in how people see you. Nothing here says her job dominates her identity.

p: A status is a position in society, like professor or mother. A role is the set of behaviors expected from someone in that position.
One status usually has several roles attached. That bundle is the role set. All the statuses one person holds together make the status set.

x8C_003.eli: Think of a video game character (status: 'knight'). The knight has several jobs: fight, guard the gate, protect the king. Those jobs together are the role set.
mem: Status = position; role = expected behavior
Role set = many roles, ONE status
Status set = many statuses, ONE person
x8C_003.trap: Students swap 'role set' and 'status set'. Ask: is it many roles for one position, or many positions for one person?
x8C_003.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Achieved statuses are earned or chosen, like being a doctor. The prince did nothing to get his title.
Wrong. 'Instrumental' describes group ties built around a goal or task. It is not a type of status, so it is a vocabulary distractor.
Correct. An ascribed status is assigned at birth or by others, without effort. Royal title, sex and ethnicity are classic examples.
Wrong. Role exit is leaving a role. He has not left anything, and it is not a status type.

p: A status is a social position. An ascribed status is given to you, usually at birth, and you cannot easily change it. An achieved status is something you earn or choose through effort.
Examples: ascribed is age, sex, race, royal birth. Achieved is being a surgeon or a college graduate.

x8C_004.eli: Ascribed is like the color of your eyes, you were handed it. Achieved is like a trophy you won.
mem: Ascribed = assigned, no effort
Achieved = earned or chosen
Birth-based titles are ascribed
x8C_004.trap: The prince will later perform duties, which tempts you toward 'achieved'. The question asks how he got the status, not what he does with it.
x8C_004.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Status inconsistency means a person holds statuses with very different prestige. Physician is high, her stigmatized group membership is low, so people treat her in mixed ways.
Wrong. Role exit means leaving a role. She is still a physician, so no exit happened.
Wrong. Role strain is competing demands within ONE role. Her problem is unequal prestige between TWO statuses.
Wrong. Her physician status is achieved, but 'achieved master status' does not name a clash between statuses. The clash is the point of the question.

p: Every status has a level of prestige, or social respect. Status inconsistency happens when one person has statuses with very different prestige levels.
Others may then react unpredictably, respecting one status while looking down on another.

x8C_006.eli: It is like being the school's best player but also the new kid nobody sits with. Some people cheer, others ignore you.
mem: Status inconsistency = mismatched prestige across statuses
Role strain = one role, competing demands
Role conflict = two roles, competing demands
x8C_006.trap: Role strain sounds right because she feels pressure. But strain is about demands, not prestige mismatch.
x8C_006.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Role conflict needs demands from two DIFFERENT statuses, like resident and parent. Here two audiences ask different things, but both ask about the one status of resident.
Correct. Role strain is tension among expectations of a single status. Be fast (attendings) and be thorough (patients) are both parts of being a resident.
Wrong. Role exit is leaving a role. The resident is still in training and not quitting.
Wrong. Role reversal means two people trade positions. Nobody swaps places here.

p: Role strain is stress from clashing expectations within one status. Role conflict is stress from clashing expectations between two different statuses.
To tell them apart, count the statuses involved, not the number of people asking.

x8C_008.eli: A cashier told to go faster and to chat with each customer has strain: one job, two rules. A cashier whose boss wants overtime while her kid's school wants her home has conflict: two jobs.
mem: Strain = ONE status
Conflict = TWO statuses
Count statuses, not audiences
x8C_008.trap: Two audiences makes you think 'conflict'. Check whether both demands belong to the same status.
x8C_008.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. The turning point is the stage where the person decides to leave, and it comes after alternatives are weighed.
Wrong. Creating the ex-role is the last stage, when the person builds a new identity after leaving.
Wrong. Anticipatory socialization means rehearsing a role you hope to join. It is a general concept, not one of Ebaugh's four stages.
Correct. Ebaugh's order is first doubts, then searching for alternatives, then turning point, then creating the ex-role.

p: Role exit is the process of leaving a role that was central to your identity, such as a job or marriage. Ebaugh described four stages.
Doubts come first. Then the person looks at other options. Then a turning point triggers the decision. Finally the person builds a new ex-role identity.

x8C_010.eli: Like leaving a sports team: you start to feel unsure, you look at other hobbies, one day you decide to quit, then you become 'the former player'.
mem: Order: doubt, search, turning point, ex-role
Turning point = the decision moment
Ex-role = new identity after leaving
x8C_010.trap: The turning point feels like the dramatic next step, but the person must first weigh alternatives.
x8C_010.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. A workplace department exists to get tasks done, so it is a secondary group.
Wrong. A class is temporary, impersonal and goal-focused, which describes a secondary group.
Correct. A family is small, close, long-lasting and valued for the relationship itself. That is a primary group.
Wrong. A national association is large and formal, with members who rarely know each other. It is secondary.

p: A primary group is small and close. Members care about each other for their own sake, and ties last for years. This is called expressive, meaning based on feelings.
A secondary group is larger, more impersonal and formed to do a task. This is called instrumental, meaning goal-focused.

x8C_012.eli: Your family is like your home team you stick with forever. A class is like a group project partner you forget after the semester.
mem: Primary = small, intimate, lasting, expressive
Secondary = large, impersonal, goal-based, instrumental
Family and close friends = primary
x8C_012.trap: Coworkers can become friends, but the group itself is still task-based, so choose the family.
x8C_012.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. In the minimal group paradigm, even random labels make people favor their own group. Mere categorization is enough.
Wrong. Realistic conflict theory needs real competition for scarce resources. These groups never competed.
Wrong. A reference group is a standard people use to judge themselves. Here they were giving money, not comparing themselves.
Wrong. Primary groups are close and long-lasting. These were strangers with arbitrary labels.

concept.t: In-group favoritism and the minimal group paradigm
p: Your in-group is the group you belong to. Out-group is everyone else. In-group favoritism is treating your own group better.
Tajfel's minimal group studies used meaningless labels, such as dot-counting style. People still favored their own label. So simply being sorted into a group can create bias.

x8C_014.eli: Hand out red and blue stickers at random and kids soon want to help the kids with their own color.
mem: Minimal group paradigm = trivial groups still cause bias
Tajfel and social identity theory
Realistic conflict theory = bias from competition
x8C_014.trap: Money allocation sounds like competition over resources, but nobody competed. Random labels point to social identity.
x8C_014.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology/sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. A primary group is a close, lasting relationship. She only admires these students from afar.
Wrong. An out-group is a group you do not belong to or identify with. She identifies with them and wants to be like them, which fits a reference group, not an out-group.
Correct. A reference group is the group whose standards you use to judge and guide yourself, whether or not you belong to it.
Wrong. A dyad is a two-person group. It describes group size, not a source of standards.

p: A reference group is a group you compare yourself to and copy. You do not need to be a member.
People often copy the habits of a group they hope to join. This is called anticipatory socialization, meaning practicing for a future role.

x8C_015.eli: A kid who wants to join the soccer team copies how the team practices. The team is the kid's yardstick.
mem: Reference group = your yardstick, membership optional
Dyad = 2 people, triad = 3 people
Anticipatory socialization = rehearsing a future role
x8C_015.trap: Do not assume 'admired' means 'close'. Closeness is primary group; a standard is reference group.
x8C_015.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Density is how connected members inside a cluster are. Removing a link between clusters does not change that.
Wrong. Weak or bridging ties are often vital because they carry information between groups. This is the trap of thinking weak means unimportant.
Wrong. Removing the only link separates the clusters further. It cannot merge them.
Correct. She is the only bridge across a structural hole. Without her, information cannot pass from ICU to pharmacy.

p: A social network is a map of people and their ties. A cluster is a tightly connected group. A bridge is a tie that is the only connection between two clusters.
The gap between clusters is a structural hole. Losing the bridge cuts off information flow.

x8C_022.eli: Two islands joined by one rope bridge. Cut the bridge and nobody can cross.
mem: Bridge = only link between clusters
Structural hole = gap between clusters
Weak ties spread new information (strength of weak ties)
x8C_022.trap: Do not think a single person is unimportant. In networks, the lone connector is often the most important.
x8C_022.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Weber's model hires by technical qualifications. Family connections are what bureaucracy is designed to remove.
Wrong. Bureaucracy uses formal, standard procedures. Flexible, informal choices go against the ideal type.
Correct. Weber listed hierarchy of authority, written rules, division of labor, impersonality and merit-based hiring.
Wrong. Bureaucracy is impersonal. Emotional ties are the opposite of the model.

p: A bureaucracy is a large organization run by formal rules. Weber described an ideal type, meaning a clean model of its key features, built for efficiency and fairness.
Features: chain of command, written rules, specialized jobs, impersonal treatment, and hiring by skill.

x8C_024.eli: Like a big school: principal, teachers, written rules, everyone has a set job, and rules apply the same to every kid.
mem: Hierarchy, written rules, division of labor
Impersonality
Merit-based hiring and promotion
x8C_024.trap: Distractors describe family-style or informal groups. Bureaucracy means rules over relationships.
x8C_024.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Michels' iron law of oligarchy says even democratic organizations tend to end up ruled by a small elite.
Wrong. McDonaldization is about efficiency and standardization in society, not who holds power.
Wrong. Ritualism is following rules rigidly while forgetting goals. The stem is about power concentrating in a few people.
Wrong. Strength of weak ties is about information flow through loose connections in a network.

p: Oligarchy means rule by a few. Michels argued that as organizations grow, they need coordination and expertise, so a small group of leaders takes control.
This happens even in groups founded on equal voting.

x8C_025.eli: A class club where everyone votes equally, but over time the same three kids make every plan because they know how everything works.
mem: Michels = iron law of oligarchy
Large organizations drift to rule by a few
Happens even in democratic groups
x8C_025.trap: Names are the trap: match Michels to oligarchy, Ritzer to McDonaldization, Weber to bureaucracy.
x8C_025.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Predictability means standard, uniform experiences everywhere. The stem is about counting patients, not sameness.
Wrong. Control means using technology or rules to limit worker choices. No such limits are described.
Wrong. Efficiency is choosing the fastest route to a goal. Here the focus is on measuring quantity over quality, which is a different dimension.
Correct. Calculability means valuing what can be counted, such as patients per hour, over quality.

p: McDonaldization is the spread of fast-food style rules into society. It has four dimensions: efficiency, calculability, predictability and control.
Calculability stresses numbers. Quantity is easy to count, so it is valued over quality.

x8C_026.eli: A teacher who grades only on how many pages you wrote, not how good they are.
mem: Four parts: efficiency, calculability, predictability, control
Calculability = quantity over quality
Efficiency = fastest method
x8C_026.trap: Efficiency feels broad and tempting. If the stem says counting or measuring numbers, pick calculability.
x8C_026.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Calculability is about quantity over quality. No counting is mentioned.
Wrong. Predictability is uniform results. Uniform output may follow, but the stem highlights limiting what pharmacists can do.
Correct. Control means machines or rules replace human judgment and dictate each step.
Wrong. Efficiency is about speed to a goal. The stem never mentions speed, only limits on workers.

p: Control means using nonhuman technology, scripts or rules to direct how workers act. It reduces the need for human judgment.
An automated machine that dictates every step is a classic example.

x8C_027.eli: Like a video game with a rule at every step so you can only press the one button it lights up.
mem: Control = technology limits worker choices
Calculability = quantity
Predictability = sameness everywhere
x8C_027.trap: Predictability tempts because machines make results uniform, but the stem asks what is stressed: limiting workers.
x8C_027.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Coercive organizations, like prisons, hold members against their will. Volunteers join freely.
Correct. Normative organizations draw members through shared values or a mission, with no pay.
Wrong. Utilitarian organizations give pay or material rewards, like a company. Volunteers get none.
Wrong. A primary group is small and intimate. A hospital program is a formal organization.

p: Etzioni sorted formal organizations by why people join. Normative means members join for shared values. Utilitarian means they join for pay. Coercive means they are forced.
Volunteer groups are normative.

x8C_029.eli: Kids who join a recycling club because they care are normative. Kids paid for chores are utilitarian. Kids sent to detention are coercive.
mem: Normative = values
Utilitarian = pay
Coercive = force
x8C_029.trap: A hospital might sound like a utilitarian workplace, but volunteers are not paid.
x8C_029.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. In Goffman's model, the front is the setting, appearance and manner used to define the performance for the audience.
Wrong. Back stage is where performers relax out of view. Props meant to impress patients are the opposite.
Wrong. The audience is the people watching, in this case patients.
Wrong. A role set is the roles tied to one status. Coat and decor are props, not roles.

p: Goffman compared social life to theater. People are actors giving performances to an audience.
The front includes the setting (office), appearance (white coat) and manner (tone). It tells the audience who you are.

x8C_032.eli: A school play: costume and stage set make the audience believe the actor is a king.
mem: Front = setting, appearance, manner
Back stage = relax, drop the act
Impression management = controlling how others see you
x8C_032.trap: Do not confuse props (front) with the people watching (audience).
x8C_032.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Front stage is where staff perform for patients. Patients cannot enter this room.
Correct. Back stage is where people drop their public role, joke and vent, away from the audience.
Wrong. A reference group is a standard people compare themselves to. It is not a place.
Wrong. A total institution, like a prison, controls all parts of residents' lives. A staff room does not.

p: In Goffman's theater idea, front stage is where you perform your role for an audience. Back stage is where the audience cannot see, so you can relax.
Impression management is controlling how you appear on front stage.

x8C_033.eli: Waiters act polite in the dining room, then joke and slump in the kitchen.
mem: Front stage = performing for audience
Back stage = private, drop the act
Total institution = controls all of life (Goffman too)
x8C_033.trap: Total institution is also a Goffman term, so it looks attractive. But it is about full control of residents, not a break room.
x8C_033.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The tactical self is the self you present to match what others expect. She does not feel like a collaborator, but the company wants one, so she shows that face.
The authentic self is who she believes she truly is. Privately she dislikes teamwork, so that is her real self, not what she is showing. Mistake: picking the self she hides.
The ideal self is who she wants to become. She has no wish to be a collaborator; she is only acting like one. Trap: confusing an aspiration with a performance for an audience.
The looking-glass self (Cooley) is a self-image built from imagining how others judge us. Here she is deliberately managing an impression, not forming her self-concept from others' views.

p: Impression management is how we shape what others think of us. Three selves are named. The authentic self is who you believe you really are. The ideal self is who you wish to become.
The tactical self is who you show to others to fit their expectations. It is a mask used for a goal, such as getting a job.

x8C_036.eli: It is like wearing a nice costume to a party because the host asked for costumes, even though you would rather wear pajamas.
mem: Authentic = who I really am
Ideal = who I want to be
Tactical = who I show to meet others' expectations
Looking-glass self = self formed from imagined judgments of others (Cooley)
x8C_036.trap: Ideal self sounds tempting, but she does not want the trait. She only performs it for the audience.
x8C_036.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Trap. Nonverbal communication means cues without language, like posture, facial expression, or a shrug. ASL uses words and grammar, so it is language, even though it is made with the hands.
Correct. Verbal communication means communication through language, with words and grammar. That can be spoken, written, or signed. ASL is a full natural language, so it is verbal.
Paralanguage is how something is said with the voice: tone, pitch, volume, pace. Signing is not vocal, and ASL carries the words themselves, not just vocal flavor.
Animal signaling is communication in other species, such as bee dances. ASL is a human language with grammar and syntax.

p: Verbal communication is any communication that uses a language, meaning words arranged by grammar rules. Spoken, written, and signed languages all count.
Nonverbal communication has no language structure: facial expressions, posture, gestures like a shrug. Paralanguage is the vocal side of how words are said, such as tone and pitch.

x8C_041.eli: A letter and a phone call both use words. Sign language uses words too, just with hands instead of a voice.
mem: Verbal = uses language (spoken, written, signed)
Nonverbal = body cues without language rules
Paralanguage = tone, pitch, volume of speech
ASL is a full language with its own grammar
x8C_041.trap: Do not equate verbal with vocal. Signed language is still verbal.
x8C_041.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: If expressions were entirely learned, the two cultures would not look alike when alone. Their similarity argues against this. Trap: noticing the masking and overlooking the shared baseline.
Both groups showed disgust-like faces when alone, which is consistent with disgust being a basic emotion. Nothing in the study questions that.
Paralanguage is vocal quality such as tone and pitch. The study looked at facial expressions, not the voice.
Correct. Similar faces when alone suggest universal basic expressions. Masking in front of an authority shows cultural display rules, which are norms about when and how to show emotion.

p: Ekman found that basic emotions such as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, and disgust have facial expressions that people across cultures recognize.
Display rules are cultural norms about when it is proper to show an emotion. They can make people hide, shrink, or exaggerate the face. So the feeling is shared, but the showing is shaped by culture.

x8C_044.eli: Everyone winces at a bad smell. But in some families you must smile politely at Grandma's cooking anyway.
mem: Basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust
Expressions are largely universal (Ekman)
Display rules = cultural norms for showing emotion
Alone = true expression; with others = display rules apply
x8C_044.trap: The masking tempts you toward 'learned', but the matching faces when alone show a universal core.
x8C_044.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: A costly behavior that persists across a population usually has an adaptive function. Wasting energy near a predator would be selected against if it did nothing. Trap: calling odd behavior an accident.
Luring predators toward relatives would lower the gazelle's inclusive fitness, so selection would not favor it. Stotting actually discourages chasing.
Correct. By the handicap principle, a costly signal is honest because only a fit gazelle can afford to waste energy. The predator learns it would be hard to catch and may give up.
A pheromone is a chemical signal. Stotting is a visual display, a jump, not a chemical.

p: A signal is a behavior or trait that sends information to another animal. The handicap principle says a signal that is costly to produce stays honest, because weak animals cannot afford to fake it.
Stotting costs energy and time. Only a healthy gazelle can do it well, so it tells the predator that chasing will fail.

x8C_051.eli: It is like a kid doing a big backflip to show the bully they are too strong to pick on. Only a strong kid could do it.
mem: Costly signal = honest signal (Zahavi's handicap principle)
Only fit individuals can afford the cost
Signals can be visual, chemical (pheromone), auditory, or tactile
Persistent costly traits usually have adaptive value
x8C_051.trap: Do not treat a costly-looking behavior as pointless. Cost is what makes the signal believable.
x8C_051.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (behavioral biology and psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The swaying bridge raised heart rate and other arousal. The men labeled that arousal as attraction to the interviewer, which is misattribution of arousal, in line with the two-factor theory.
Mere exposure means liking something more from repeated contact. Both groups met her once for a similar time, so exposure did not differ.
Proximity means physical closeness. Both groups met her face to face, so closeness was the same in both.
It was the high, swaying bridge that caused more arousal, not the stable bridge. This option reverses the conditions.

p: Two-factor theory says an emotion has two parts: bodily arousal plus a mental label for it. The label depends on what is around you.
On a scary bridge, the body is aroused from fear. If a woman is standing there, the brain may label the racing heart as attraction. This is misattribution of arousal (Dutton and Aron).

x8C_058.eli: Your heart pounds on a roller coaster, and the person next to you suddenly seems extra exciting. You blamed the wrong cause.
mem: Two-factor theory (Schachter-Singer): arousal + cognitive label
Dutton and Aron bridge study = misattribution of arousal
High scary bridge = more arousal = more calls
Mere exposure = liking from repeated contact
x8C_058.trap: Do not pick mere exposure or proximity. Those were equal across groups; only arousal differed.
x8C_058.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Catharsis predicts that watching or acting out aggression drains aggressive urges. Here the children who saw aggression hit more, the opposite of catharsis.
Correct. Children copied what the adult model did. Learning by watching and imitating others is observational learning (Bandura's Bobo doll studies).
Frustration-aggression says aggression follows blocked goals. No frustration was created; the groups differed only in what they watched.
Instinct would predict similar aggression in both groups regardless of what they saw. The difference came from the model, which points to learning.

p: Observational learning means learning by watching another person, called a model, and then copying the behavior. No reward to the learner is required.
In Bandura's Bobo doll studies, kids who saw an adult hit the doll hit it more themselves. Because the groups differed only in what they saw, the watching caused the change.

x8C_061.eli: A little kid sees a big sibling stomp in puddles and then stomps in puddles too. Nobody taught them directly.
mem: Bandura = observational learning / social learning
Bobo doll: modeled aggression gets imitated
Catharsis predicts a decrease; data showed an increase
Frustration-aggression = blocked goal leads to aggression
x8C_061.trap: Catharsis sounds reasonable, but it predicts less aggression after watching. The data went the other way.
x8C_061.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Low serotonin and a weak prefrontal cortex (the brain's brake) mean impulses from the amygdala are poorly controlled, which fits impulsive aggression.
High serotonin and strong prefrontal activity mean better impulse control, so they go with less impulsive aggression. This option reverses the direction.
Lower testosterone and a smaller amygdala response both point toward less aggression. Trap: mixing up which direction each factor pushes.
Oxytocin is mainly tied to bonding and trust. It is not the main marker of impulsive aggression.

p: The amygdala generates fast emotional reactions such as anger. The prefrontal cortex is the planning area that holds those reactions back. Serotonin is a brain chemical that helps calm and regulate mood and impulses.
When serotonin is low and the prefrontal cortex is weak, the brake is poor, so anger turns into action quickly.

x8C_062.eli: The amygdala is the gas pedal and the prefrontal cortex is the brake. A weak brake means the car lurches forward.
mem: Low serotonin = more impulsive aggression
Weak prefrontal control = less inhibition
High amygdala reactivity and higher testosterone = more aggression
Oxytocin = bonding
x8C_062.trap: Watch the direction of each factor. Low serotonin raises aggression, while low testosterone lowers it.
x8C_062.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and neuroscience texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Catharsis predicts that aggression would drop after venting. No venting happened, and the rifle group shocked more.
Instrumental aggression is harm used to reach another goal, like robbing someone for money. The shocks were not tied to another goal.
Correct. A rifle is an aggressive cue that primes aggressive thoughts. In angry people, this raises the chance of aggression. This is the weapons effect (Berkowitz and LePage).
Social facilitation is better performance on easy tasks when others are present. The presence of other people was not what was varied.

p: Priming means that seeing one thing makes related ideas easier to think of. A weapon in view can prime aggressive thoughts.
If a person is already angry, those primed thoughts make aggressive acts more likely. This is the weapons effect.

x8C_064.eli: If you see a pile of cookies, you suddenly think of cookies. If you see a weapon when you are mad, you think of fighting.
mem: Weapons effect = weapons are aggressive cues
Cues prime aggressive thoughts
Works best when the person is already aroused or angry
Instrumental aggression = aggression to get something else
x8C_064.trap: Do not choose instrumental aggression. Look for the object that triggers aggression by priming.
x8C_064.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: A bigger survey is still a correlation. It cannot rule out third variables or reverse causation, so it cannot show the games cause aggression.
Correct. Random assignment makes the groups alike on average, so only the game type differs. A later difference in aggression can then be blamed on the games, which supports causation.
Asking aggressive teens why they like games gives opinions and only a correlation. People are poor at explaining their own causes.
Parents' attitudes add another variable but no control over who plays what. This still cannot test cause.

p: A correlation means two things go together. It does not prove one causes the other. Reverse causation means the effect might be the cause, for example aggressive teens choosing violent games. A third variable could also drive both.
An experiment with random assignment places people into groups by chance. That spreads other differences evenly, so a group difference can be linked to the manipulated factor.

x8C_066.eli: Umbrella carriers and wet streets go together, but umbrellas do not make rain. To test causes, you must hand umbrellas out at random.
mem: Correlation does not equal causation
Random assignment + manipulation = causal inference
Third variable and reverse causation are the usual alternatives
More surveys do not fix a correlational design
x8C_066.trap: A bigger sample sounds stronger, but size does not turn a correlation into a cause.
x8C_066.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (research methods in psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Avoidant infants show little distress at separation and ignore the caregiver when she returns. This infant was upset and greeted her warmly, so that does not fit.
Ambivalent infants are upset but hard to soothe and may resist comfort when the caregiver returns. This infant was quickly soothed.
Disorganized infants show confused, contradictory behavior, such as freezing or approaching and then backing away. This infant behaved in a clear, consistent way.
Correct. Secure infants use the caregiver as a secure base. They are upset at separation, glad at reunion, and easily comforted.

p: Ainsworth's Strange Situation watches how a baby reacts when the caregiver leaves and returns. The reaction shows the attachment style.
Secure: upset on leaving, happy and soothed on return. Avoidant: little upset, ignores caregiver. Ambivalent: upset, but cannot be calmed. Disorganized: confused and contradictory.

x8C_068.eli: A secure kid cries when Mom leaves, then runs to hug her and feels better. An ambivalent kid hugs and then pushes her away.
mem: Secure: distress, welcome, quickly soothed
Avoidant: little distress, ignores caregiver
Ambivalent: distress, resists comfort
Disorganized: confused, contradictory behavior
x8C_068.trap: Both secure and ambivalent infants are upset. The deciding clue is how easily they calm down.
x8C_068.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Operant conditioning shapes behavior through reward or punishment. Goslings follow the object without any reinforcement being given.
Kin selection is behavior that helps relatives. The goslings follow any moving object, even a person, so it is not aimed at kin.
Correct. Imprinting is rapid, fixed learning of attachment to the first moving object seen, but only inside a short critical period after hatching (Lorenz).
Secure attachment is a classification of human infants in the Strange Situation. Imprinting is a different, quick, animal process tied to a critical period.

p: Imprinting is a fast form of learning in which a young animal bonds to the first moving thing it sees. A critical period is a limited time window in which this learning must happen.
Lorenz showed goslings would follow him as if he were their mother. It needs no reward and is not about family.

x8C_074.eli: It is like baby ducklings thinking the first thing they see is Mom, and the window to choose closes fast.
mem: Imprinting = rapid attachment to first moving object (Lorenz)
Happens in a critical period
No reinforcement needed
Not specific to kin
x8C_074.trap: Do not pick operant conditioning or kin selection. Imprinting needs neither reward nor relatives.
x8C_074.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (behavioral biology and psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Negative-state relief says people help to reduce their own bad feelings. If that were true, easy escape would also relieve distress, so high-empathy people would leave. They stayed and helped.
Correct. Empathic concern produced real altruism: high-empathy people helped even when leaving was easy. Low-empathy people helped mainly when escape was hard, which looks egoistic (Batson).
Kin selection means favoring relatives to pass on shared genes. The student was a stranger, not a relative.
Frustration-aggression explains aggression after blocked goals. It says nothing about helping.

p: Altruism is helping another person without a selfish payoff. Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis says that feeling empathy, meaning sharing someone's feelings, produces a true desire to help for their sake.
Without empathy, people help mostly for their own reasons, such as avoiding guilt. Test: make escape easy. Egoistic helpers leave; empathic helpers still help.

x8C_078.eli: A friend who cares about you helps even when they could sneak away. Someone who only wants to avoid feeling bad helps only when stuck.
mem: Empathy-altruism (Batson): empathy leads to true altruism
Easy escape + still helping = altruism
Negative-state relief = helping to feel better yourself
Kin selection = helping relatives
x8C_078.trap: The egoistic option is tempting, but it predicts that easy escape lowers helping for everyone.
x8C_078.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (social psychology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: If everyone is a dove, a single hawk takes resources easily and does better, so hawks invade. All-dove is not stable.
If everyone is a hawk, fights are costly and injuries common. A dove avoids fights and can do better, so doves invade. All-hawk is not stable.
Correct. Since neither pure strategy resists invasion, the stable result is a mix of hawks and doves, with proportions set by fight costs and the resource's value.
Invasion does not wipe out strategies. Each does well when it is rare, so both persist.

p: An evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) is one that, once common, cannot be beaten by a rare alternative. Hawks fight hard for resources. Doves display and give up.
Rare hawks beat doves, and rare doves beat costly hawk fights. So each does well when rare, and the population settles on a stable mix.

x8C_080.eli: If everyone shares, a greedy kid wins. If everyone is greedy, they fight and nobody wins, so a sharer does better. You end up with both kinds.
mem: ESS = cannot be invaded by a rare alternative
All-dove is invaded by hawks
All-hawk is invaded by doves
Result: a stable mix of both
x8C_080.trap: Do not assume one strategy must win. When each beats the other while rare, a mix is stable.
x8C_080.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (behavioral ecology and game theory texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: The direct (main) effect says support helps health at all stress levels. These data show little effect under low stress, so this does not fit.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis is about aggression after blocked goals, not about health or support.
Correct. The buffering hypothesis says support protects mainly by cushioning stress. The benefit appears in high-stress people, an interaction between stress and support.
The iron law of oligarchy says organizations become ruled by a small elite. It has nothing to do with health.

concept.t: Buffering vs. direct effect of social support
p: Social support means help and caring from other people. The buffering hypothesis says support protects health mainly when stress is high, by cushioning its harm.
The direct effect hypothesis says support helps health no matter how stressed you are. The key is who benefits: only stressed people means buffering.

x8C_083.eli: Rain gear helps only when it rains. Buffering is like that: support matters most in the storm.
mem: Buffering: support helps mostly under high stress
Direct effect: support helps at all stress levels
Buffering = stress x support interaction
Iron law of oligarchy = organizational power
x8C_083.trap: Check who benefits. If low-stress people gain nothing, it is buffering, not a main effect.
x8C_083.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (health psychology and sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Trivers' parental investment theory says the sex that invests more per offspring is choosier. In pipefish males carry the eggs, so males are choosy and females compete.
Pipefish show the opposite pattern, with competing females. So males are not always the competitive sex.
Mating behavior follows parental care closely. The pipefish reversal in roles matches the reversal in care.
In pipefish, males invest more by brooding. So females do not always invest more.

p: Parental investment is the time, energy, and risk a parent spends on each offspring. Trivers said the sex that invests more has more to lose from a bad mate, so it is choosier.
The sex that invests less competes for access to mates. It is investment, not being male or female, that sets the pattern.

x8C_089.eli: The one who has to do the most homework picks their partner most carefully. The other kid just races to be picked.
mem: More investment = choosier sex
Less investment = competes for mates
Usually females invest more; pipefish reverse it
Roles follow investment, not sex
x8C_089.trap: Do not memorize 'males compete, females choose' as a fixed rule. Follow who invests more.
x8C_089.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (behavioral ecology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Direct benefits are things the chooser gets herself, like food, territory, or help raising young. He provides none of these.
Kin selection is about helping relatives. He is her mate, not her relative.
Correct. Bright plumage signals parasite resistance, a sign of good genes. Passing those genes to her young is an indirect genetic benefit.
Reciprocal altruism is trading favors over time. No favors are exchanged in this scenario.

concept.t: Direct vs. indirect benefits of mate choice
p: Direct benefits go to the chooser herself, such as food, a nest site, or parental care. Indirect benefits are good genes passed to her offspring, which makes them healthier.
Bright plumage can be an honest sign of health, such as resisting parasites. If the male gives nothing else, her only gain is better genes for her young.

x8C_090.eli: Picking a dad with strong, healthy genes is like picking a seed from the best plant, even if the plant gives you no fruit now.
mem: Direct = food, territory, care
Indirect = good genes for offspring
Bright ornaments can signal health
Kin selection and reciprocal altruism are different ideas
x8C_090.trap: The key clue is 'provides no food or nest'. That rules out direct benefits.
x8C_090.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (behavioral ecology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Explicit prejudice means consciously held, openly reported attitudes. She reports none. The trap is reading any negative result as 'prejudice' without asking whether it is conscious.
Wrong. Institutional discrimination is unfair treatment built into an organization's policies. A lab test of one person involves no policy.
Wrong. Individual discrimination is unfair behavior toward someone. Only reaction times were measured, not treatment of anyone. The trap is mixing up an attitude with an action.
Correct. The IAT measures automatic mental links by speed. Faster 'old' + negative pairing shows a hidden association, even though she sincerely reports no negative feelings.

p: Explicit attitudes are beliefs you know you have and can report. Implicit attitudes are automatic links in your mind that you may not notice.
The Implicit Association Test (IAT) times how fast you pair a group with good or bad words. Faster pairing means a stronger mental link. The two kinds of attitude can disagree.

x8C_096.eli: Your head can have a habit, like reaching for the light switch in the wrong room, that you would never say you believe in.
mem: IAT = reaction-time test of implicit (automatic) associations
Implicit can differ from explicit (self-reported) attitudes
Attitude (prejudice/bias) is not the same as behavior (discrimination)
x8C_096.trap: Do not call every negative result prejudice or discrimination. The question says she denies negative feelings, so the answer must allow a gap between hidden and stated attitudes.
x8C_096.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. An all-weather liberal has no prejudice and does not discriminate. This owner does discriminate. The trap is noticing 'no prejudice' and stopping there.
Wrong. A timid bigot is prejudiced but does not discriminate. This owner is the reverse: not prejudiced, but he acts against the group.
Wrong. An active bigot is prejudiced and discriminates. The owner explicitly holds no prejudice.
Correct. Fair-weather liberal (unprejudiced discriminator): no personal prejudice, but he discriminates because of customer pressure.

p: Merton crossed two questions: Is the person prejudiced (an attitude)? Does the person discriminate (an action)? That gives four types.

Prejudiced and discriminates: active bigot. Prejudiced but does not act: timid bigot. Not prejudiced and does not act: all-weather liberal. Not prejudiced but acts anyway under pressure: fair-weather liberal.

x8C_097.eli: A kid who likes the new student but won't sit with them because the popular kids would tease him.
mem: Active bigot = prejudice + discrimination
Timid bigot = prejudice, no discrimination
All-weather liberal = neither
Fair-weather liberal = no prejudice, but discriminates
x8C_097.sc: Name the attitude first, then the action. The adjective (liberal or bigot) tells you the attitude; 'fair-weather' or 'timid' tells you the behavior is shaped by circumstance.
x8C_097.trap: Mixing up the two liberal types. 'Fair-weather' means the good attitude disappears under pressure, so he discriminates.
x8C_097.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Seniority layoffs look neutral, but because women were excluded earlier they have less seniority, so past discrimination still causes harm today.
Wrong. Individual discrimination is one person treating another unfairly out of bias. Here a company-wide policy causes the effect and no one is acting on bias now.
Wrong. Implicit bias is an automatic mental association in a person. The disparity comes from a rule, not from anyone's associations.
Wrong. Prejudice is an attitude, not a layoff practice. The trap is choosing the familiar word instead of the one that describes a policy outcome.

p: This is a type of institutional discrimination. A rule that seems fair today carries forward the effects of unfair treatment in the past.
Seniority means years of service. If women were kept out for decades, they have fewer years, so last-in-first-out layoffs hit them hardest.

x8C_098.eli: Imagine a race where some kids were held back at the start for years. Now everyone is told to run at the same speed, but the held-back kids are still far behind.
mem: Past-in-present = neutral rule, effects of earlier discrimination
It is a form of institutional discrimination
No current biased individual is required
x8C_098.trap: Choosing individual discrimination because someone is harmed. Look for who acts: a policy, not a biased person.
x8C_098.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Owners said they would refuse, but almost all served the couple. So prejudice did not always lead to discrimination. The trap is assuming attitudes always become actions.
Wrong. The study looked at individual owners' behavior and statements, not organizational policies, so it says nothing about institutional discrimination.
Correct. Stated attitudes (the mail replies) did not match behavior (service nearly always given). This is LaPiere's classic attitude-behavior gap.
Wrong. The study did not measure implicit associations. Owners reported stated attitudes by mail. The trap is using a trendy term the data cannot support.

p: LaPiere traveled with a couple from a minority group and was refused service only once. Later, most owners said by mail they would refuse such customers.
So what people say about a group often does not predict what they actually do. Attitudes and behavior can differ.

x8C_100.eli: A kid says he hates broccoli, then eats it at dinner without a fuss. What people say and do can differ.
mem: LaPiere: stated attitudes did not predict behavior
Prejudice (attitude) does not always lead to discrimination (action)
Study measured explicit statements, not implicit bias
x8C_100.trap: Assuming the mail replies show real behavior. Behavior was the actual service, which was nearly always given.
x8C_100.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (psychology and sociology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.
